newsitem.title: JAPAN: "VIP accounts" at heart of widening Nomura scandal.
newsitem.headline: "VIP accounts" at heart of widening Nomura scandal.

text.p: At the heart of the widening payoff scandal facing Nomura Securities is the question of whether it offered "VIP accounts" in the true sense of the word.
The scandal took a twist with possible political repercussions on Tuesday when the chief government spokesman said three cabinet ministers held accounts at the brokerage.

Japanese media reports have charged that "VIP accounts" offered preferential treatment to selected customers. Nomura denied the existence of such special accounts and argued the term was not applied to mean "Very Important Persons."
Nomura said they had started using the word "VIP" as a label for certain customers from 1983, when they computerised their system supervising client information.
The firm said it had stopped using the term from April to avoid any further "misunderstanding" about its usage.
"The account and the term however are not meant at all to offer any preferential treatment in business transactions with our company," Nomura said in a statement issued in March.
Other Japanese brokerages said they did not categorize their clients, except maybe to differentiate between firms and individuals which operate under separate tax laws.
"There's absolutely no categorization of customers. I've never heard of such practice (like a VIP account) at other brokerages either," said an employee of a major Japanese securities firm.

The existence of VIP accounts at Nomura became known after a former Nomura employee told the Japanese media in fall of 1996 that Nomura offered preferential treatment to selected clients holding such special accounts.
Politicians, senior bureaucrats and business leaders were among those said to be holding VIP accounts at Japan's largest brokerage firm, according to media reports.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference on Tuesday that three cabinet members currently had "dealings" with Nomura, but said they were not getting preferential treatment.
Nomura, which initially denied the existence of VIP accounts, finally acknowledged in March that 8,000 to 9,000 customers out of its five million customers held so-called "VIP accounts."

Former Nomura President Hideo Sakamaki told parliament the following month that accounts were labeled "VIP" if those clients needed careful treatment such as when sending direct mail about transactions.

Tokyo prosecutors, who arrested three former Nomura executives for their alleged shady dealings with a former racketeer, are said to be looking closely into whether there was more to being a VIP account holder than a noisy customer.
Media reports said that VIP account holders are said to be able to get their hands on financial products which are more likely to create profits, such as convertible bonds.
The reports cited industry sources to say that about 90 percent of all financial products invested by VIP account holders are convertible bonds.

Convertible bonds can be converted to shares after a certain period, and an investor can make a profit if the share price rises above the price of the bond, which is based on the value of the share at the time the bond is launched.

Industry sources say major Japanese brokerages would refrain from buying certain shares before issuing a convertible bond of that particular firm, hoping to see the share price rise after launching the bond.
Prosecutors have already seized a list of the VIP account holders during the raids, and Sakamaki told parliament Nomura was willing to cooperate if authorities demanded a list of its customers.
